items.q: A count-min sketch reports that #monsoon has 3,877 views. What do you know about the true count?

options.t: It is at most 3,877
options.why: Right. Collisions can only add to a cell, never subtract, and the read takes the minimum across rows — so the estimate is an upper bound. The truth is 3,877 or less.

options.t: It is at least 3,877
options.why: Backwards. That would be true of a structure that undercounts. Count-min only ever inflates, so 3,877 is the ceiling, not the floor.

options.t: It is within 1% either way
options.why: That's HyperLogLog's two-sided error. Count-min's error is one-directional and its size depends on the sketch width and the total event volume, not a fixed percentage.

options.t: Nothing without knowing the hash functions
options.why: The one-directional guarantee holds for any hash functions. The hashes affect how much it overshoots, not which way.

items.q: Why does a count-min sketch always need a min-heap beside it for top-K?

options.t: The sketch scores a key you hand it; it can't list the big ones
options.why: Exactly. The sketch stores no keys — only collided counters. The heap remembers who the current big keys are; the sketch tells you how big.

options.t: The heap stores exact counts, which correct the sketch's estimates before ranking
options.why: The heap stores estimates that came from the sketch, so it inherits the same error. It solves the 'which keys' problem, not the accuracy problem.

options.t: The heap is needed to expire old counts
options.why: Expiry comes from tumbling buckets — you discard a whole bucket. The heap is about identity, not time.

options.t: The heap protects against hash collisions
options.why: Collisions are handled by using several rows and taking the minimum. The heap has no role in that.

items.q: How do two count-min sketches with identical width, depth and hash functions merge?

options.t: Add the cells element-wise
options.why: Right — a cell holds a count of occurrences, and occurrences in two disjoint streams add. The merged sketch equals what one machine would have built seeing every event.

options.t: Take the element-wise maximum
options.why: That's how HyperLogLog merges, where each bucket holds a longest-run-of-zeros. Taking the max of counts would throw away the second stream's events.

options.t: Bitwise OR
options.why: That's Bloom filter merging, where cells are single bits. OR-ing counters is meaningless arithmetic.

options.t: They can't merge — you must recount from the raw events
options.why: Mergeability is the whole reason sketches suit sharded systems. It's the entry requirement for any structure you plan to compute in parallel.

items.q: Why is a sliding one-hour window built from 60 tumbling one-minute sketches instead of one long-lived sketch?

options.t: Counters only go up, so old events can't be removed — you discard whole buckets
options.why: Correct. Decrementing would corrupt every other key sharing those cells. Bucket-and-discard is the only clean expiry, and the cost is that the window edge moves in one-minute steps.

options.t: Sixty small sketches together use less memory than one sketch sized for a whole hour
options.why: The opposite: 60 buckets cost 60x the memory of one. You pay that deliberately to buy expiry.

options.t: Small sketches have smaller error
options.why: Per-bucket error is smaller because each holds fewer events, but summing 60 buckets adds their errors back. Expiry is the reason, not accuracy.

options.t: Kafka delivers data in one-minute batches
options.why: Nothing about Kafka forces a bucket size. The bucket length is your choice, traded off against memory and window granularity.

items.q: What is the main memory advantage of a count-min sketch over an exact hash map for this problem?

options.t: Its size is fixed and does not grow with the number of distinct keys
options.why: That constant is the whole argument. A billion junk keys invented by a spammer cost the sketch zero extra bytes, while the exact map grows on demand at the attacker's convenience.

options.t: It compresses the keys so they take less space
options.why: It doesn't store keys at all — compressed or otherwise. That's also why it can't enumerate them back to you.

options.t: It keeps only the top K keys in memory and discards everything below the cutoff
options.why: That's the heap's job. The sketch holds counters for every key that has ever been added, all overlapping in a fixed grid.

options.t: It stores counters on disk instead of RAM
options.why: It's an in-memory structure. Its trick is sharing cells between keys, not moving anywhere cheaper.

items.q: What separates a 'most viewed' list from a 'trending' list?

options.t: Trending ranks by rate of change against a baseline; most-viewed ranks raw volume
options.why: Right. Volume gives you milk-and-bread forever; trending is a derivative — what's rising unusually fast for itself. Same counters, two different scores.

options.t: Trending uses a shorter window
options.why: A shorter window still returns the biggest things in that window. Without a baseline comparison, you've just made a fresher volume list.

options.t: Trending is exact while most-viewed is approximate
options.why: Both come from the same approximate counters here. The difference is the scoring function, not the accuracy.

options.t: Trending is personalized to each user's follows and watch history, most-viewed is global
options.why: Personalization is a separate product feature layered on top. An unpersonalized trending list is still velocity-based.

items.q: The leaderboard takes 1M reads/sec. How does the design absorb that?

options.t: Reads hit a small cached blob at the edge, never the counting pipeline
options.why: Exactly. The list is a tiny precomputed document; the counting fleet publishes it every few seconds and never sees a user request. Cost: the displayed number is a few seconds stale.

options.t: The aggregator answers each request by querying the sketch ring and re-ranking on the fly
options.why: That would put a million sketch queries per second on the fleet to produce an answer that is identical for everyone. Precompute once, serve many.

options.t: Requests are sharded across the 32 shard workers
options.why: Shards are sized for the write path. Sending reads there couples user-facing latency to the counting hot loop — precisely what you want to avoid.

options.t: The batch job serves reads from the warehouse table
options.why: The warehouse is for exact analytics queries, not 1M/sec of home page renders, and it's an hour behind.

items.q: In the estimation, which number was the one that ruled out the exact hash map?

options.t: About 240 GB of hot RAM for 60 minute-buckets of exact counters
options.why: That's the number that forced the sketch. Note how it was derived: distinct keys per minute times bytes per entry times 60 buckets, all said out loud before any structure was chosen.

options.t: 10M events per second at peak
options.why: Volume drives shard count and CPU, but volume alone doesn't kill a hash map — you can count fast in a map. It's the distinct-key count that explodes memory.

options.t: 1M leaderboard reads per second
options.why: That shapes the serving layer (a cached blob), not the counting structure.

options.t: Tens of terabytes of raw events a day, retained for the batch path
options.why: That sizes the object-storage log for the batch path, where disk is cheap. It doesn't decide the in-memory structure.

items.q: Why does the exact batch path exist alongside the streaming path?

options.t: Payouts need exact counts, which replaying a lossy stream can't produce
options.why: Right. The batch job is a different algorithm, not a re-run — it can afford exactness because it may spend minutes and disk. It also sees late events that the stream's window already closed.

options.t: Because streaming systems drop messages under load, so financial numbers can't be trusted
options.why: A properly checkpointed stream doesn't lose data. The stream here is inexact because the sketch deliberately discards information, not because delivery is unreliable.

options.t: To provide a backup if Kafka fails
options.why: Both paths read the same Kafka stream, so it's no protection against Kafka. The batch path buys exactness, not redundancy.

options.t: Because batch jobs are cheaper to run
options.why: The batch tier is extra cost and a second codebase computing the same thing — the lambda tax. It's justified by an exactness requirement, not by savings.

items.q: Three regions each send their local top-1000 heap to a global aggregator. A hashtag is rank 3 in India and around rank 400 in the US and Brazil. What happens if you merge only the heaps?

options.t: It appears with only India's count, so it ranks far below its true position
options.why: Right — and the fix is union-then-re-query: take the candidate keys from every heap, then look each one up in the merged sketch to recover the counts the other regions never reported.

options.t: It's dropped entirely, since it isn't in every heap
options.why: A sane merge keeps the union of keys, not the intersection. The bug isn't that it disappears — it's that it carries a partial count.

options.t: Nothing — heap merging is exact as long as every region counts its own traffic correctly
options.why: Each region has a genuine partial count, and partial counts don't rank correctly against each other. Heap merging is only sound when a key lives entirely on one node.

options.t: Its count is doubled because it appears in multiple heaps
options.why: Different regions counted different events, so adding them is correct arithmetic. The problem is the counts you never received, not double counting.

items.q: You partition events by hash of the key, and one video takes 1% of a 10M/sec stream — 100K events/sec to a single shard. Is this the classic hot-partition disaster?

options.t: No — sketch updates are constant-cost with no state growth, and pre-aggregation folds the burst
options.why: Exactly the nuance. Hot keys kill you when they grow state or serialize on a lock; here the per-event work is four increments into a fixed array. 100K/sec is a few percent of a core.

options.t: Yes — that shard's sketch will grow until it runs out of memory
options.why: The sketch is a fixed-size array. Its footprint is identical whether one key gets everything or a billion keys share it evenly.

options.t: Yes — switch to round-robin partitioning so the load spreads evenly across all 32 shards
options.why: That trades a non-problem for a real one: round-robin splits each key across all shards and makes per-shard top-K unsound. You'd need full sketch merging to recover.

options.t: No, because Kafka automatically rebalances hot partitions
options.why: Kafka does no such thing — a keyed partition's traffic is determined by the key hash. The reason this is safe is the constant per-event cost, not a broker feature.

items.q: Your hour-window overshoot bound is about 11,000. The 10th-ranked key has ~1M views; the 1000th has ~60,000 with neighbours within a couple of percent. What do you tell the product team?

options.t: The top 10 is stable; treat the tail of the top 1000 as a set, not a ranking
options.why: This is the crux applied: error only matters where the gap at the boundary is smaller than the error. Naming which part of the list is trustworthy — rather than defending all of it — is the senior move.

options.t: The whole list is accurate to within about 1%
options.why: 11,000 on 1M is 1%; on 60,000 it's 18%. Quoting one relative error for a power-law list hides the only place the error actually bites.

options.t: The list is unreliable and shouldn't be published until the counts come from the batch path
options.why: Over-correction. The head is safe by orders of magnitude, and the head is what most users see. Scope the caveat to the tail.

options.t: Widen the sketch until the list is exact
options.why: Widening helps and is cheap, but no width makes it exact. If a surface needs exactness, it reads the batch table — that's what the second path is for.

items.q: A key was rank ~400 in every one of the last 60 minute-buckets, so it never entered any bucket's top-1000 output. Should it appear in the hourly top 100?

options.t: It should — candidates come from the heaps, but scores come from summing all 60 sketches
options.why: Right. Per-bucket heap membership says nothing about hourly rank. The heaps generate candidates (rank 400 is comfortably inside a top-1000 heap); the sketches produce the hourly score.

options.t: No — if it never topped a minute, it can't top an hour
options.why: Steady mid-tier volume compounds. Sixty consistent minutes can beat one enormous spike, and a design that can't see this misses whole categories of trends.

options.t: Only if you also keep a separate hour-length sketch running alongside the minute ring
options.why: You could, but you'd lose sliding expiry — the hour sketch can't forget its oldest minute. Summing the ring gives the same answer with correct expiry.

options.t: Yes, and the heaps alone are enough to find it
options.why: Half right. It's in the heaps, so candidate generation finds it — but its rank must come from summing 60 sketch estimates, not from heap positions.

items.q: Your velocity score is recent_rate / baseline_rate. A brand-new hashtag goes from 2 mentions to 40 and tops the trending list. What's the fix?

options.t: A volume floor: only keys already in the top ~10,000 by count can be ranked
options.why: Right. Candidate generation by volume, ranking by velocity. A 20x ratio on tiny numbers is noise, and every ratio-based score needs this guard.

options.t: Rank by the absolute increase instead of the ratio, so tiny keys can't dominate
options.why: That turns trending back into a volume list — big keys have the biggest absolute deltas, so the umbrella never beats the milk.

options.t: Increase the sketch width so small counts are accurate
options.why: The counts weren't wrong; 2 and 40 may be exactly right. The scoring function is what's broken, not the counter.

options.t: Lengthen the window to an hour
options.why: A tiny key over a longer window is still a tiny key with a wild ratio. Window length doesn't address division by small numbers.

items.q: A hundred bot accounts push one hashtag a thousand times each. What in the design notices, without a full spam-classification system?

options.t: Rank the top candidates by distinct users (a HyperLogLog each), not by event count
options.why: Exactly. 100K events from 100 users collapses to 100. You only pay for HLLs on the ~10K candidates that clear the volume floor — about 120 MB — and HLLs merge across regions by per-bucket max.

options.t: The count-min sketch, because repeated identical events collide
options.why: Collisions have nothing to do with repetition. The sketch counts occurrences faithfully and cannot tell 100K bot events from 100K human ones.

options.t: The batch job, since exact counts reveal bots
options.why: Exact counting of bot events gives you an exactly wrong trending list. Exactness and authenticity are different problems.

options.t: Rate limiting at the API gateway, so no single account can post the same tag repeatedly
options.why: Useful, and worth having — but per-account limits don't stop a hundred accounts each acting within limits. The counting metric has to change.

items.q: The aggregator process dies. What's the recovery story you'd describe?

options.t: A new leader with a fencing token re-merges the shards' summaries in seconds
options.why: Right. Everything the aggregator knew still exists in the shards' sketch rings, so recovery is a re-merge, not a rebuild from raw events. The fencing token stops a revived old aggregator from overwriting with stale output.

options.t: Replay the Kafka log from the beginning of the hour through a new aggregator
options.why: Unnecessary work — the shards already hold the aggregated per-minute state. Replay is the shard's recovery path, not the aggregator's.

options.t: The leaderboard goes unavailable until the next hourly batch job completes and republishes
options.why: An hour of blank trending for a process restart would be a terrible design. The cached blob covers the gap, and the re-merge takes seconds.

options.t: Nothing to do — the aggregator is stateless
options.why: Close, but too breezy. It holds merged window state and is the single writer of the published blob; the honest phrasing is 'stateless enough to rebuild', plus fencing to make the handover safe.

items.q: Which metric would catch a silently drifting approximation that latency, CPU and error-rate dashboards would all miss?

options.t: Daily overlap@K between the published list and the batch job's exact top-K
options.why: This is the correctness alarm. A drifting sketch produces plausible-looking lists with perfect operational metrics — only comparison against ground truth exposes it.

options.t: Publish lag from bucket close to blob write
options.why: Measures freshness, not truth. A pipeline can publish a wrong list on time, every time, with lag looking beautiful.

options.t: Kafka consumer lag per partition, alerted when any partition falls behind by a minute
options.why: Catches a stalled or under-provisioned consumer. Says nothing about whether the numbers being computed are right.

options.t: Sketch memory usage
options.why: It's a fixed-size array — the memory number is a constant by construction, which makes it one of the least informative metrics in the system.

items.q: Traffic goes 10x, to 100M events/sec. What happens to the sketch?

options.t: Memory is unchanged, but absolute error grows 10x with volume — so widen the rows
options.why: The sharp answer. Overshoot is roughly (e/w) x N, so 10x the events means 10x the overshoot even though the footprint never moved. Ten times the width costs a few hundred MB — trivial — and restores the boundary.

options.t: Memory grows 10x with the traffic
options.why: The grid is fixed-size. Confusing 'more events' with 'more memory' misses the exact property that made sketches the right choice.

options.t: Nothing changes; the sketch is scale-free
options.why: Half true and dangerously incomplete. Memory is scale-free; accuracy is not. That distinction is precisely what a 10x probe is fishing for.

options.t: Error shrinks in relative terms, because more events smooth the collision noise across cells
options.why: More events mean more collisions piling into every shared cell. Volume inflates the overshoot, it doesn't average it away.

items.q: Interviewer: 'You're already streaming everything through Flink. Why not drop the batch tier and just replay the stream when you need to fix numbers?' Best response?

options.t: "Replay gives the same approximation back — the sketch already threw that information away. Batch is a different algorithm, one that can afford exactness. Drop the exactness requirement and I'd delete the tier."
options.why: Names the real reason (lossy by construction, not unreplayable), adds the late-event argument, and volunteers the condition under which the extra tier should be deleted. Committing while stating what would change your mind is the senior shape.

options.t: "Lambda architecture is the industry standard for analytics pipelines — every large company runs a batch layer beside its streaming one to correct the numbers, so I'd keep both paths and let the batch view win on conflict."
options.why: Appeal to fashion, and out of date — kappa is the modern default. The interviewer asked for a mechanism and got a label.

options.t: "Good point, we could probably drop it. Let's go with one streaming path."
options.why: Folding at the first push abandons a requirement you committed to ten minutes earlier. Payouts still need exact counts, and replay won't produce them.

options.t: "Streaming can't be trusted for financial data because messages get lost under load, so anything that pays out has to be recomputed from the durable log by a separate batch job."
options.why: Factually shaky — checkpointed streams don't lose data — and it hides the actual argument. Defending a good decision with a wrong reason invites a probe you'll lose.

items.q: You have 20 minutes of deep-dive time on this problem. Which topic is the true crux to claim first?

options.t: The output is an ordering, so overestimate-only error corrupts ranks near K
options.why: This is the burning room. Everything else is assembly; this is the part where approximation meets a user-visible decision, and it's the only part where you must produce arithmetic to defend the design.

options.t: How the load balancer routes ingest traffic to collectors
options.why: Solved, routine, and identical in every system in this book. Spending deep-dive minutes here is touring the room with the curtains.

options.t: Whether the leaderboard blob lives in Redis or Memcached, and how to size that cluster for a million reads a second
options.why: A one-line decision about a document that's a few kilobytes. Real, trivial, and not what the question was invented to probe.

options.t: The JSON schema of the trending API response
options.why: The API section should take two minutes. Two fields there matter (as_of and estimated) and they're honesty flags, not a deep dive.

items.q: Product wants K = 5 for a home page module, and your sketch's hour overshoot is ~11,000 counts. The top 5 keys have 2M, 1.8M, 900K, 880K and 870K views. What do you commit to?

options.t: Ship it — 11,000 against gaps of tens of thousands is safe, though ranks 4 and 5 may swap
options.why: Committing with the arithmetic, and flagging the one genuinely close pair rather than claiming blanket accuracy. Ranks 4 and 5 are ~10,000 apart, which is inside the bound — knowing that, and saying it, is the whole skill.

options.t: Refuse until the counts are exact, since the module is user-facing
options.why: User-facing isn't the same as payable. Blocking a display list on exactness costs 240 GB of RAM to prevent an occasional swap between ranks 4 and 5 that no user can detect.

options.t: Widen the sketch until the overshoot is under 100 counts, whatever the memory bill turns out to be
options.why: Over-engineering by reflex. You'd be buying three orders of magnitude of precision for a decision that needed one — and never checking whether the gap made it unnecessary.

options.t: Serve the module from the batch table instead
options.why: That's an hour-stale trending list on the home page — trading a rare rank swap for a guaranteed staleness bug. The requirement was near-real-time.

items.q: Halfway through the interview you realize your minute-ring design gives you one-minute window granularity, but you promised 10-second freshness. How do you handle it?

options.t: Raise it yourself: the open bucket counts as it fills, so freshness is seconds even though the window edge steps by a minute — and 10-second buckets cost 6x the ring if that's not enough
options.why: Self-caught gap, precise distinction between window granularity and freshness, and a costed fix if the distinction doesn't satisfy. Catching your own hole before the interviewer does is worth more than not having the hole.

options.t: Say nothing — one minute is close enough to 10 seconds
options.why: It's also a different thing, and the interviewer is likely to notice. An unflagged mismatch between a stated requirement and the design is exactly the gap they're hunting for.

options.t: Restate the freshness requirement as one minute so it matches what you've already drawn on the board, and carry on to the next section
options.why: Quietly moving the goalposts to fit the design is the opposite of engineering. Renegotiating a requirement out loud with a reason would be fine; retconning it isn't.

options.t: Scrap the ring and rebuild the windowing around exponentially decayed counters, which slide continuously with no bucket boundary at all, then re-present the design from the top
options.why: Throwing out a working mechanism under mild pressure reads as panic — and decay means periodically rescaling every counter and blurring the window boundary. Adjust the bucket size, don't restart.

items.q: New requirement: advertisers pay for placement in the trending module, so the published list must be exact and auditable. Strongest response?

options.t: "Exactness is affordable once the key set is bounded — exact counters for the ~100K registered campaigns (10 MB), sketch for the open tail, plus idempotency keys so retries can't inflate a paid count."
options.why: Finds the real principle: the sketch was never about counting being hard, it was about unbounded keys. Bound the set and exact becomes trivial. The idempotency note is the tell of someone who has counted money before — at-least-once delivery becomes a correctness bug the moment counts pay out.

options.t: "Then we need exact counting for everything — I'd shard an exact key-value store across enough machines to hold every distinct key in the window, accept the memory bill, and have finance fund the extra fleet."
options.why: Applies the new constraint to a billion keys when it only applies to a hundred thousand. Paying 240 GB per scope to satisfy a requirement about registered advertisers is over-engineering with a straight face.

options.t: "Keep the sketch, and add a disclaimer that counts are approximate."
options.why: A disclaimer is not an audit. Once placement is paid for, 'our estimator overshoots by up to 11,000' is a legal conversation, not an engineering one.

options.t: "Widen the sketch until the error is negligible for the paid keys."
options.why: No width makes it exact, and 'negligible' isn't auditable. Worse, it spends real memory to get almost the property you could have had exactly, for less, by bounding the key set.

items.q: Publish lag 4s, zero errors, CPU normal — and the trending list has shown identical items for three hours. Where do you look first?

options.t: At content production: is the ring pointer advancing, is the oldest bucket being zeroed
options.why: Right, and the ordering is the reasoning. Healthy lag and TTL rule out the transport half, so the fault is upstream — a stuck ring or a reset that stopped running turns the 'hour' into an ever-growing all-time count, which barely changes and looks frozen.

options.t: At the CDN, since the users are clearly seeing a cached copy
options.why: Possible, but the publish-lag metric says fresh blobs are being written — so the cache is likely serving new content that happens to be identical. Check where content is made before where it's moved.

options.t: At Kafka, since consumer lag is the usual cause of stale data
options.why: Consumer lag would show as growing publish lag and stale as_of timestamps. Both are healthy, which is what makes this failure interesting.

options.t: Restart the aggregator, since a stuck internal timer is the usual cause and a restart clears it
options.why: Restarting before diagnosing destroys the evidence for a bug that will come back. It's also the reflex that skips the real finding here: nothing alerted, because no monitor compared the output to reality.

items.q: Another team switches Kafka to round-robin partitioning to balance load. Nothing errors, the leaderboard still renders. What do you say?

options.t: "That silently breaks the merge — every key is now split 32 ways, so mid-ranked ones never enter any local heap. Give me key-hash partitioning back, or I switch to sketch-merge plus re-query."
options.why: Names the mechanism, the repair, and the scariest part: a well-intentioned change by another team degraded correctness with no error, no alert, and a plausible-looking list. That last observation is the on-call maturity signal.

options.t: "Fine — round-robin balances producer load better, and the aggregator merges every shard's output before publishing anyway, so the final list comes out the same either way."
options.why: Only true if the aggregator merges sketches and re-queries candidates. If it was doing a cheap heap merge (which key-hash partitioning made valid), the output is now quietly wrong.

options.t: "Revert it. Partitioning is our decision, not theirs."
options.why: Right instinct, wrong delivery, and no mechanism. Reverting without explaining what breaks means the change comes back next quarter with a different justification.

options.t: "Add more shards to compensate for the smearing."
options.why: More shards make it worse — each key is split even more finely, so more genuine keys drop out of every local heap.
